content: Insomnia is a significant public health concern, affecting approximately 6% to 10% of adults in Western countries. Eszopiclone is a hypnotic medication classified as a new-generation hypnotic agent. It has been marketed as being equally effective as benzodiazepines for treating insomnia, while purportedly offering a safer profile with a lower risk of abuse and dependence. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of eszopiclone by analyzing evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), while also considering methodological quality and potential biases. The objective of the review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of eszopiclone in treating insomnia, comparing it to either a placebo or an active control. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, PSYNDEX, and clinical trial registries, with the most recent search update performed on February 21, 2018. Additional efforts were made to identify unpublished trials by contacting key informants and reviewing reference lists of relevant studies. Studies identified in the update search were classified as awaiting further evaluation or ongoing and will be included in future updates of the review. The review included parallel-group RCTs that compared eszopiclone to placebo or active controls. Participants were adults diagnosed with insomnia using standardized diagnostic criteria, encompassing both primary insomnia and insomnia comorbid with other conditions. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, with one assessing trial quality and the other cross-checking the results. A total of 14 RCTs involving 4,732 participants were included in the review. These studies examined the short-term (≤4 weeks; 6 studies), medium-term (>4 weeks to ≤6 months; 6 studies), and long-term (>6 months; 2 studies) effects of eszopiclone. Most participants were aged 18 to 64 years, although three studies exclusively included elderly individuals (aged 64 to 85 years), and one study included a broader age range (35 to 85 years). Seven studies focused on primary insomnia, while the remaining studies addressed secondary insomnia associated with conditions such as depression, generalized anxiety, back pain, Parkinson's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and menopausal transition. Meta-analyses of participant-reported sleep outcomes demonstrated that eszopiclone was more effective than placebo. Specifically, eszopiclone reduced sleep onset latency by an average of 12 minutes (mean difference [MD] -11.94 minutes, 95% confidence interval [CI] -16.03 to -7.86; 9 studies, 2,890 participants, moderate-quality evidence). It also decreased wake time after sleep onset by 17 minutes (MD -17.02 minutes, 95% CI -24.89 to -9.15; 8 studies, 2,295 participants, moderate-quality evidence) and increased total sleep time by 28 minutes (MD 27.70 minutes, 95% CI 20.30 to 35.09; 10 studies, 2,965 participants, moderate-quality evidence). There was no significant evidence of rebound insomnia or worsening of sleep parameters in the first three nights after discontinuing eszopiclone. For example, changes in sleep onset latency (MD 17.00 minutes, 95% CI -4.29 to 38.29; 1 study, 291 participants, low-quality evidence) and wake time after sleep onset (MD -6.71 minutes, 95% CI -21.25 to 7.83; 1 study, 291 participants, low-quality evidence) were not statistically significant. Adverse events were more frequently reported in participants taking eszopiclone compared to placebo. These included unpleasant taste (risk difference [RD] 0.18, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.21; 9 studies, 3,787 participants), dry mouth (RD 0.04, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.06; 6 studies, 2,802 participants), somnolence (RD 0.04, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.06; 8 studies, 3,532 participants), and dizziness (RD 0.03, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.05; 7 studies, 2,933 participants). According to the GRADE criteria, the quality of evidence was rated as moderate for sleep efficacy outcomes and adverse events, but low for rebound effects and next-day functioning. In conclusion, eszopiclone appears to be an effective treatment for improving sleep onset and maintenance in individuals with insomnia, with a moderate effect size. When used as recommended, the drug demonstrated minimal evidence of harm. However, certain patient populations, such as those with cognitive or motor impairments and those at risk of misuse, were underrepresented in the included RCTs. Therefore, caution is advised when prescribing eszopiclone to these groups, particularly elderly individuals.
